title: MOH weighs HFMD vaccine strategy as cases plunge 83% - The Vibes

analysis.time: The Health Ministry is assessing the potential role of an HFMD vaccine, with the latest update on Aug 26, 2026. The review comes amid a steep decline in HFMD cases this year, with a 83% drop compared to the previous year.
analysis.location_and_population: Malaysia, with the focus on young children aged between six months and six years, who are primarily affected by HFMD.
analysis.event: The Ministry of Health (MOH) is evaluating whether vaccination should be part of its strategy against HFMD, noting that the available vaccine targets only EV-A71, which accounts for 1.5% of detected enteroviruses in Malaysia this year.
analysis.scale_impact_and_risk: Malaysia records tens of thousands of HFMD cases annually, with a 266% surge in the first quarter of last year compared to 2024. However, cases have since dropped by 83% this year, with 40,879 cases reported as of Aug 22, 2026. The vaccine's potential role is being assessed against the broader pattern of HFMD transmission, which is mainly driven by other viruses like Coxsackievirus A6 and A16.
analysis.response_status_and_uncertainty: The MOH is reviewing the need and appropriate role of HFMD vaccination in Malaysia, with the National Pharmaceutical Regulatory Agency currently assessing a vaccine imported from China. The ministry will continue to monitor the HFMD situation and emerging scientific evidence.

analysis.brief_en: The Ministry of Health (MOH) in Malaysia is evaluating the potential role of an HFMD vaccine, as cases have dropped by 83% this year compared to the previous year. The available vaccine targets only EV-A71, which accounts for 1.5% of detected enteroviruses in the country, while most infections are caused by other viruses like Coxsackievirus A6 and A16. The ministry is considering the broader epidemiological context of HFMD, which mainly affects young children aged six months to six years. A local pharmaceutical company is seeking to import and market an HFMD vaccine from China, with plans for local production. The National Pharmaceutical Regulatory Agency is currently reviewing the vaccine, and the MOH will continue to monitor the situation and emerging scientific evidence. The review comes amid a significant decline in HFMD cases, raising questions about the vaccine's public health value in Malaysia.
analysis.summary_en: The Ministry of Health (MOH) in Malaysia is evaluating the potential role of an HFMD vaccine, as cases have dropped by 83% this year compared to the previous year. The available vaccine targets only EV-A71, which accounts for 1.5% of detected enteroviruses in the country, while most infections are caused by other viruses like Coxsackievirus A6 and A16. The ministry is considering the broader epidemiological context of HFMD, which mainly affects young children aged six months to six years. A local pharmaceutical company is seeking to import and market an HFMD vaccine from China, with plans for local production. The National Pharmaceutical Regulatory Agency is currently reviewing the vaccine, and the MOH will continue to monitor the situation and emerging scientific evidence. The review comes amid a significant decline in HFMD cases, raising questions about the vaccine's public health value in Malaysia.

analysis.brief_en: The Star reports that a vaccine against hand, foot and mouth disease (HFMD) is available in China and targets the EV-A71 strain, which is one of the many enteroviruses that can cause HFMD. However, healthcare professionals state that it is not yet time to include the vaccine in Malaysia's National Immunisation Programme due to its limited effectiveness against other common HFMD viruses like Coxsackievirus A16. The ministry has found that EV-A71 accounts for just 1.5% of the enteroviruses detected so far, though there is a noted shift towards this strain. Malaysia has recorded 40,879 HFMD cases this year, with the vaccine potentially reducing severe infections and mortality. Despite its benefits, the vaccine does not prevent all HFMD cases, and there are concerns about possible side effects. The Health Ministry is currently studying the feasibility of including the vaccine in the national immunisation schedule, which outlines mandatory shots for infants and children against diseases such as tuberculosis, diphtheria, tetanus, polio, measles, and mumps. The vaccine is considered a critical tool for managing recurring HFMD epidemics, but its inclusion remains under review.
